questions.title: Fix the loop
questions.text:
```pseudocode
Total ← 0
FOR i FROM 0 TO LENGTH(Score)
    Total ← Total + Score[i]
ENDFOR
```

Explain the error in this code and how to correct it.

scheme.model_answer: The loop goes one index too far: Score[LENGTH(Score)] is outside the upper bound, giving a run-time error. The loop should be FOR i FROM 0 TO LENGTH(Score) − 1.

questions.title: Move the first element
questions.text:
The array QUEUE stores N names. The first person in the queue has to move to the **end**, e.g. [Ali, Bota, Dina, Erlan] becomes [Bota, Dina, Erlan, Ali].

Write pseudocode or program code to do this.

scheme.mark_scheme: Save the first element in a temporary variable (1); loop with the correct range from 0 to N − 2 / forwards (1); QUEUE[i] ← QUEUE[i + 1] (1); put the saved element in QUEUE[N − 1] (1)
scheme.model_answer:
```pseudocode
Buf ← QUEUE[0]
FOR i FROM 0 TO N - 2
    QUEUE[i] ← QUEUE[i + 1]
ENDFOR
QUEUE[N - 1] ← Buf
```

questions.title: Row totals
questions.text: The 2D array Sales[0:11, 0:4] stores the sales of 5 shops (columns) for each of 12 months (rows). Write pseudocode or program code that outputs the total sales of **each shop**.

scheme.mark_scheme: Outer loop over the shops / columns 0 to 4 (1); total reset to 0 for each shop (1); inner loop over the months 0 to 11 adding Sales[m, s] (1); output the total after the inner loop (1)
scheme.model_answer:
```pseudocode
FOR s FROM 0 TO 4
    Total ← 0
    FOR m FROM 0 TO 11
        Total ← Total + Sales[m, s]
    ENDFOR
    OUTPUT "Shop ", s, ": ", Total
ENDFOR
```

parts.title: Move to the end
parts.text:
The array TASKS stores N tasks. A worker must start the day with the task that is currently **last**: e.g. [task1, task2, task3, Meeting] becomes [Meeting, task1, task2, task3].

Write pseudocode or program code that rearranges the array.

scheme.mark_scheme: buf ← TASKS[N − 1] (1); loop from N − 1 down to 1 (1); TASKS[i] ← TASKS[i − 1] (1); TASKS[0] ← buf (1)
scheme.model_answer:
```pseudocode
Buf ← TASKS[N - 1]
FOR i FROM N - 1 DOWNTO 1 STEP -1
    TASKS[i] ← TASKS[i - 1]
ENDFOR

```

summary: What an array is and why it is better than many separate variables; array terminology — identifier, element, index, lower and upper bound, length, dimension, zero-based indexing and out-of-range errors; declaring and processing 1D arrays (traversal, total, maximum, search, swap, shift); 2D arrays — rows, columns, row and column totals, nested loops; parallel arrays; and choosing a suitable 1D or 2D array for a given task.

blocks.content: A **data structure** that stores a **fixed number** of elements of the **same data type** under **one identifier** (name). Each element is accessed by its **index** (position).

blocks.title: Separate variables or one array?
rows: 30 different names to declare and remember
Every value must be written out separately
A **loop** can process every element using the index
Adding a 31st value means changing the code

items.title: Why a programmer uses an array
items.content:
- Only **one identifier** is needed for many values.
- It is **easy to iterate** over the elements with a loop and an index.
- Code is **shorter**, easier to read and to maintain.
- It is an **efficient** way of storing many values of a similar type — the elements are stored **next to each other** in memory.
- It is **quicker to search and sort** an array than a set of separate variables.

items.title: Properties of an array
items.content:
- **Homogeneous** — all elements have the **same data type** (all INTEGER, all STRING…).
- **Static** (in pseudocode) — the size is fixed when it is declared.
- **Ordered** — every element has a position; the order is kept.
- **Random (direct) access** — any element can be reached at once by its index, e.g. `Score[17]`, without reading the others → **O(1)**.

blocks.caption: An array in memory — elements are stored in consecutive locations

blocks.title: Technical terms
rows: One value stored in the array
The position number used to access an element
The number of indexes needed to locate one element
The type that every element has

blocks.content: The **lower bound** is the index of the **first** element and the **upper bound** is the index of the **last** element. Number of elements = **upper bound − lower bound + 1**.

blocks.title: Bounds depend on how indexing starts
Exam convention
blocks.content: NIS exams usually use **0-based** arrays (like Python): an array of length **N** has minimum index **0** and maximum index **N − 1**. If the question declares bounds, e.g. `ARRAY[1:10]`, use those.

DECLARE Score : ARRAY[0:4] OF INTEGER            // 1D, 5 integers
DECLARE Name  : ARRAY[0:29] OF STRING            // 1D, 30 strings
DECLARE Marks : ARRAY[0:29, 0:5] OF INTEGER      // 2D, 30 rows × 6 columns

Score ← [56, 71, 43, 90, 88]                     // initialise with values
Score[2] ← 45                                     // change one element
OUTPUT Score[LENGTH(Score) - 1]                   // last element → 88
blocks.caption: Declaring arrays in pseudocode

blocks.content:
score = [56, 71, 43, 90, 88]      # a list used as an array
score[2] = 45                     # change one element
print(score[len(score) - 1])      # last element → 88
names = [""] * 30                 # 30 empty strings
marks = [[0] * 6 for _ in range(30)]   # 30 rows × 6 columns
blocks.caption: The same in Python

blocks.content: Using an index **below the lower bound** or **above the upper bound** (e.g. `Score[5]` when the upper bound is 4) causes a **run-time (execution) error** — the program is syntactically correct but crashes while running. A common cause is a loop `FOR i FROM 0 TO LENGTH(Score)` that should stop at `LENGTH(Score) − 1`.
Visiting **every element** of an array in turn, usually with a `FOR` loop from the **lower bound** to the **upper bound**.

Total ← 0
FOR i FROM 0 TO LENGTH(Score) - 1
    Total ← Total + Score[i]
ENDFOR
Average ← Total / LENGTH(Score)
OUTPUT Total, Average
blocks.caption: Total and average

blocks.content:
Max ← Score[0]
Pos ← 0
FOR i FROM 1 TO LENGTH(Score) - 1
    IF Score[i] > Max THEN
        Max ← Score[i]
        Pos ← i
    ENDIF
ENDFOR
OUTPUT "Highest ", Max, " at index ", Pos
blocks.caption: Largest value and its position

blocks.content:
INPUT Target
Index ← -1
i ← 0
WHILE i <= LENGTH(Names) - 1 AND Index = -1
    IF Names[i] = Target THEN
        Index ← i
    ENDIF
    i ← i + 1
ENDWHILE
OUTPUT Index
blocks.caption: Linear search — index of a value, or -1

items.title: Comparing adjacent elements
items.content:
- Neighbours are `ARR[i]` and `ARR[i + 1]`.
- **Not in ascending order:** `IF ARR[i] > ARR[i + 1]` — the condition used in bubble sort.
- The loop must stop at `LENGTH(ARR) − 2`, otherwise `ARR[i + 1]` is out of range.

items.title: Swapping two elements
items.content:
- Needs a **temporary** variable:
- `Temp ← A[i]`, `A[i] ← A[j]`, `A[j] ← Temp`.
- Without `Temp`, the first value would be overwritten and lost.

blocks.title: Shifting elements — move the last element to the front
blocks.content:
The array `ACTIVITIES` = [task1, task2, task3, Break] must become [Break, task1, task2, task3].

```pseudocode
N ← LENGTH(ACTIVITIES) - 1           // upper bound
Buf ← ACTIVITIES[N]                  // save the last element (Break)
FOR i FROM N DOWNTO 1 STEP -1
    ACTIVITIES[i] ← ACTIVITIES[i - 1]  // move each element one place right
ENDFOR
ACTIVITIES[0] ← Buf                  // put Break at the front
```
The loop must go **backwards** — going forwards would copy task1 into every position.

blocks.title: Updating two arrays — a substitution
blocks.content:
`fieldP` holds the 11 players on the field and `subP` the 3 substitutes. To replace player `s1` with substitute `s2`:

```pseudocode
INPUT s1, s2
FOR i FROM 0 TO 2
    IF subP[i] = s2 THEN
        FOR j FROM 0 TO 10
            IF fieldP[j] = s1 THEN
                subP[i] ← fieldP[j]       // the player leaves the field
                fieldP[j] ← s2            // the substitute comes on
            ENDIF
        ENDFOR
    ENDIF
ENDFOR
```
An array that needs **two indexes** to locate an element — usually **[row, column]**. It can be thought of as a **table** or **grid**, or as an array of 1D arrays.

blocks.title: Row totals and column totals of the Marks table

blocks.content: To process **row by row** (each student), the **row** index is the outer loop. To process **column by column** (each test), the **column** index is the outer loop. The inner loop always runs completely for each value of the outer loop.

blocks.title: Selecting the structure for a task
blocks.content:
| Task | Structure | Declaration |
|---|---|---|
| Store the score of each of 25 students | **1D** | `Score : ARRAY[0:24] OF INTEGER` |
| Store the scores of 25 students in 4 tests | **2D** — row = student, column = test | `Score : ARRAY[0:24, 0:3] OF INTEGER` |
| Store a 9 × 9 sudoku grid | **2D** | `Grid : ARRAY[0:8, 0:8] OF INTEGER` |
| Store whether each of 12 rows × 20 seats is booked | **2D** of BOOLEAN | `Booked : ARRAY[0:11, 0:19] OF BOOLEAN` |
| Store the rainfall for each day of a year | **1D** | `Rain : ARRAY[0:364] OF REAL` |
| Store the rainfall per day for 12 cities | **2D** | `Rain : ARRAY[0:11, 0:364] OF REAL` |

Two or more **1D arrays** of the **same length** in which elements with the **same index** belong to the same item — e.g. `Name[3]` and `Score[3]` describe the same student. Used when the data items have **different data types** (a STRING name and an INTEGER score), because one array can hold **only one** data type.

blocks.caption: Parallel arrays — the same index links the data

blocks.title: Justify your choice
blocks.content: An exam answer must give a **reason**: "A **2D array**, because each student has **several marks of the same type**, so one index is the **student (row)** and the other is the **test (column)**." Simply writing "2D array" usually earns only part of the marks.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Explain why the programmer might prefer to use an array instead of a set of variables. [2]**
Only **one name** is needed (1); it is **easy to iterate** over the elements with a loop using the index (1). Also accepted: efficient storage of many values of the same type; quicker to search.

**Q: Identify the possible minimum and maximum indexes of an array. [2]**
Minimum: **0** (1); maximum: **length of array − 1** (1).

**Q: Array fieldP stores 11 players. Determine the indexes of the first and last elements. [1]**
**0 and 10** (1).

**Q: Write a condition that checks if two adjacent elements of an array ARR are not in ascending order. [1]**
`IF ARR[i] > ARR[i + 1]` (1).

**Q: The program uses an index outside the bounds of the array. Name the type of error. [1]**
**Run-time** (execution) error (1).

- Saying the upper bound is the **length** — for 0-based arrays it is **length − 1**.
- Writing `FOR i FROM 0 TO LENGTH(A)` — the last pass is **out of range**.
- Mixing up the order of 2D indexes: say clearly which is the **row** and which is the **column**.
- Trying to store a name and a score in the **same** array — use **parallel arrays** (or a record).
- Swapping without a temporary variable, which **loses** one of the values.
- Shifting elements to the right with a **forward** loop — it copies the same value into every position.
